name: Cross Collar Choke from Body Triangle
summary: The cross collar choke from body triangle is a gi blood choke from back control where the figure-four leg lock frees both hands to feed crossed grips deep into the opponent's collar and compress both carotid arteries.
description: Master the cross collar choke from body triangle in BJJ. Learn grip mechanics, finishing details, and defensive strategies for this powerful gi submission.
overview:
The cross collar choke from body triangle combines the mechanical control advantage of the body triangle with the direct choking power of crossed collar grips. Unlike a standard rear naked choke, this attack uses the gi collar as the primary choking mechanism, making it available whenever the opponent wears a gi. The body triangle's constant rib compression forces the defender to manage breathing difficulty while simultaneously defending their collar, creating a multi-layered offensive threat that is extremely difficult to address.

From the body triangle, the attacker's legs are fully committed to lower body control through the figure-four lock, which frees both hands entirely for collar work. This is a significant advantage over hook-based back control, where one or both hands often assist with positional maintenance. The attacker feeds one hand deep into the cross-side collar with four fingers inside, then works the second hand to the opposite collar. The finish comes from pulling the elbows back toward the hips while expanding the chest, creating a scissoring action across both carotid arteries.

This submission is particularly effective as a complement to the rear naked choke and bow and arrow choke from body triangle. When the defender tucks their chin to defend the RNC, the collar grips become accessible. When they fight collar grips, the neck opens for the RNC. This creates a decision tree where every defensive choice opens a different submission pathway, making the body triangle an elite finishing platform in gi grappling.

injury_risks.injury: Carotid artery compression leading to temporary loss of consciousness
injury_risks.recovery_time: Immediate recovery if released promptly; potential for serious injury if held past unconsciousness

injury_risks.injury: Trachea damage from improper hand placement or windpipe-focused pressure
injury_risks.recovery_time: 1-2 weeks for minor irritation; months for severe tracheal damage

injury_risks.injury: Neck strain from defensive reactions against the choke

safety_considerations.application_speed: SLOW and progressive - 3-5 seconds minimum application time in training
tap_signals: Verbal tap (saying 'tap' or any verbal signal)
Physical hand tap on partner's body or mat
Physical foot tap on mat or partner
Any distress signal including facial expressions or loss of resistance
release_protocol: Immediately release both collar grips upon tap signal
Open body triangle and disengage controlling position
Allow partner space to recover breathing and circulation
Check partner's alertness and ensure full recovery before continuing
training_restrictions: Never apply full choking pressure during initial learning phases
Never hold the choke past the tap signal under any circumstances
Never use competition speed or intensity in basic drilling
Never practice on partners with neck or circulation issues without instructor supervision
Always ensure partner has clear access to tap with hands or feet despite body triangle control

attacker.name: Cross Collar Choke from Body Triangle Attacker
attacker.description: Learn to execute the cross collar choke from body triangle. Step-by-step grip mechanics, finishing sequences, and how to overcome common defenses.
attacker.overview: Attacking the cross collar choke from body triangle gives you an exceptionally stable platform for collar work. Your legs handle all positional control through the figure-four lock, freeing both hands entirely for grip fighting and choking. The breathing restriction from the body triangle creates urgency that forces your opponent into defensive errors, opening collar access. This combination of mechanical control and choking threat makes the cross collar choke from body triangle one of the highest-percentage gi finishes from back control, especially when integrated into a submission chain with the RNC and bow and arrow.
key_principles: Use the body triangle's breathing restriction to force defensive errors that expose the collar
Feed the first grip deep into the cross-side collar with four fingers inside before pursuing the second grip
Keep chest-to-back pressure constant to prevent the defender from creating space to turn and face you
Finish by pulling elbows toward your hips while expanding your chest, creating a scissoring action across both carotids
Chain collar attacks with RNC threats so every defensive response opens a different submission
Maintain the body triangle squeeze throughout the choking sequence to compound breathing restriction with blood choke pressure
setup_requirements: Established body triangle with secure figure-four lock around opponent's lower ribcage
Chest-to-back connection maintained with hips positioned on mat for stable base
At least one hand free from positional maintenance to begin collar hunting
Opponent wearing a gi with accessible collar material on both sides of the neck
Upper body control sufficient to prevent opponent from turning to face you during grip work

execution_steps.action: Secure body triangle and establish upper body control
execution_steps.description: Lock your body triangle tight around the opponent's lower ribcage with the foot deep behind your knee. Establish a seatbelt grip or over-under control with your upper body. Pulse the triangle squeeze to create breathing urgency.
execution_steps.timing: Maintain for 5-10 seconds to establish control rhythm

execution_steps.action: Feed the first deep collar grip
execution_steps.description: With your choking-side hand, reach over the opponent's shoulder and feed four fingers deep inside the cross-side collar, gripping the fabric near the back of the neck. Pull the collar tight against their neck to eliminate slack.

execution_steps.action: Consolidate first grip and set angle
execution_steps.description: Once the first grip is deep, pull your elbow down toward your hip to take up slack in the collar. Adjust your hip angle slightly to position yourself for the second hand entry. Use the body triangle squeeze to distract the defender.

Bring your other hand over or under the opponent's opposite shoulder and feed four fingers inside the collar on the other side. This creates the crossed configuration with both hands gripping opposite collars, forming an X across the throat.
execution_steps.timing: 3-6 seconds depending on opponent's hand fighting

execution_steps.description: With both grips secured, position your wrists against the sides of the opponent's neck targeting the carotid arteries. Ensure the pressure is directed to the sides of the neck rather than the front of the throat. Tighten both grips by twisting your fists.

Pull both elbows back toward your hips while simultaneously expanding your chest forward into the opponent's back. This scissoring action drives your wrists and forearms into both carotid arteries. Increase body triangle squeeze to prevent any escape attempt during the finish.
execution_steps.timing: 3-5 seconds for progressive application in training

common_counters.counter: Defender strips collar grips by two-on-one grip fighting before choke is set
common_counters.your_response: Immediately switch to RNC attempt when hands come off your wrists, as grip fighting exposes the neck. Alternate between collar and RNC threats to keep defender reactive.

common_counters.counter: Defender tucks chin deep and hunches shoulders to block collar access
common_counters.your_response: Use the body triangle squeeze to force them to address breathing, which loosens chin tuck. Alternatively, switch to bow and arrow by grabbing the collar from the bottom up rather than over the shoulder.

common_counters.counter: Defender turns toward you to face you and escape back control entirely
common_counters.your_response: Use your body triangle to prevent the turn. If they begin turning, switch to armbar as their arm becomes exposed, or transition to mounted triangle if they fully face you.

common_counters.counter: Defender reaches back to attack the body triangle lock while you work collar grips
common_counters.your_response: Their hands attacking your legs means their neck is completely undefended. Accelerate collar grip insertion and immediately apply the choke. This is a favorable exchange for the attacker.

common_errors.error: Hunting collar grips before the body triangle is fully secured and locked
common_errors.consequence: Opponent escapes back control entirely because legs were not committed to positional maintenance, wasting the collar grip setup work
common_errors.correction: Always verify the body triangle figure-four lock is tight and secure before releasing upper body grips to begin collar work

common_errors.error: Gripping the collar too shallow with only fingertips instead of deep four-finger insertion
common_errors.consequence: Shallow grips slip under pressure, require excessive hand strength to maintain, and create a windpipe choke instead of a blood choke
common_errors.correction: Feed fingers deep inside the collar past the second knuckle, grip the fabric firmly, and pull all slack out before attempting the second grip

common_errors.error: Applying pressure to the front of the throat instead of the sides of the neck
common_errors.consequence: Creates a painful but ineffective air choke that may cause tracheal injury without producing a clean submission, and gives the opponent more time to escape
common_errors.correction: Position wrists against the lateral sides of the neck and finish by pulling elbows toward hips rather than squeezing hands inward toward center

common_errors.error: Releasing body triangle squeeze pressure while focusing on collar grip work
common_errors.consequence: Removes the breathing restriction that forces defensive errors, allowing opponent to calmly address collar grips without urgency
common_errors.correction: Maintain or increase body triangle squeeze throughout the entire collar attack sequence to keep the defender under compounding pressure

common_errors.error: Attempting to finish with arm strength alone by squeezing hands together
common_errors.consequence: Arms fatigue quickly, finish is weak and escapable, and the choke relies on muscular endurance rather than mechanical advantage
common_errors.correction: Finish by pulling elbows toward hips and expanding chest forward, using back muscles and body mechanics rather than hand and forearm strength

common_errors.error: Abandoning collar attack immediately when first grip is stripped
common_errors.consequence: Fails to establish a persistent offensive cycle, allowing defender to settle into a comfortable defensive rhythm without threat
common_errors.correction: Immediately re-attempt collar grip or switch to RNC as a chain attack, maintaining constant offensive pressure rather than resetting to neutral control

training_progressions.focus: Collar grip insertion and fabric control
training_progressions.description: Practice feeding deep collar grips from body triangle on a compliant partner. Focus on four-finger insertion depth, slack removal, and proper wrist positioning against the carotid arteries. No resistance, pure technique repetition.

training_progressions.focus: Elbow retraction and chest expansion finish
training_progressions.description: With both grips established on a compliant partner, practice the finishing motion of pulling elbows toward hips while expanding chest. Develop the feeling of mechanical advantage over muscular effort. Partner provides tap feedback on choke quality.

Partner actively defends collar grips with two-on-one defense and chin tucks. Practice overcoming grip defense while maintaining body triangle control. Introduce RNC switching when collar access is denied.

training_progressions.focus: Competition-speed attack cycling from body triangle
training_progressions.description: Full resistance sparring from established body triangle. Chain cross collar choke with RNC and bow and arrow attempts based on defensive reactions. Focus on reading opponent responses and selecting the highest-percentage attack in real time.

flashcards.question: What anatomical structures does the cross collar choke from body triangle target?
flashcards.answer: The cross collar choke targets both carotid arteries on the lateral sides of the neck. The crossed wrists create a scissoring action that compresses the carotid arteries bilaterally, restricting blood flow to the brain. This is a blood choke, not an air choke, and produces unconsciousness within seconds when properly applied.

flashcards.question: Your opponent aggressively strips your first collar grip before you can secure the second - what adjustment prevents this cycle from repeating?
flashcards.answer: Immediately switch to a rear naked choke attempt when their hands leave your wrist to fight your collar grip. This creates a dilemma where defending the collar exposes the neck to the RNC, and defending the RNC exposes the collar. Chain between these two attacks so each defensive reaction opens the other submission pathway.

flashcards.question: What role does the body triangle squeeze play during the cross collar choke finishing sequence?
flashcards.answer: The body triangle squeeze restricts the opponent's diaphragm and compresses their ribcage, creating breathing difficulty that compounds with the blood choke. This dual pressure forces the opponent to address two simultaneous threats and often accelerates the tap. Maintaining or increasing the squeeze during the choke prevents the opponent from settling into calm defense.

flashcards.question: What indicators tell you the choke is correctly applied to the carotid arteries rather than the trachea?
flashcards.answer: A correctly applied blood choke produces a feeling of tightness on the sides of the neck, and the opponent may show facial color change within seconds. If the opponent is coughing, gagging, or the pressure is concentrated on the front of the throat, the choke is misapplied to the trachea. Wrist position against the lateral neck and elbow retraction toward the hips indicate correct arterial targeting.

flashcards.question: How should you release the cross collar choke from body triangle after your partner taps?
flashcards.answer: Immediately release both collar grips upon any tap signal. Then open the body triangle by unlocking the figure-four leg configuration. Allow your partner space to recover breathing and circulation. Check their alertness and ensure full recovery before continuing training. Never hold any pressure past the tap, as blood chokes can cause unconsciousness within seconds of effective application.

flashcards.question: What finishing mechanic produces the strongest choke - squeezing the hands together or pulling elbows toward the hips?
flashcards.answer: Pulling the elbows toward the hips while expanding the chest forward produces a far stronger and more sustainable finish. This uses the large muscles of the back and the mechanical advantage of chest expansion rather than forearm and grip strength. Squeezing hands together fatigues quickly and often creates tracheal pressure rather than clean arterial compression.

flashcards.question: Your opponent tucks their chin deeply to prevent collar access - what strategy opens the collar for grip insertion?
flashcards.answer: Increase the body triangle squeeze to force them to address breathing, which loosens the chin tuck as they reflexively lift their head. Alternatively, use a cross-face or jaw pressure with one hand to create space for the collar hand. You can also feed the collar grip from below the chin rather than over the shoulder, working the fingers along the jaw line into the collar.

flashcards.question: Why is it dangerous to apply this choke at full speed during training, and what is the proper application speed?
flashcards.answer: Blood chokes can cause unconsciousness in as little as 3-4 seconds when properly applied to both carotid arteries. At full competition speed, a training partner may not have adequate time to recognize the choke is locked and signal a tap before losing consciousness. The proper training application speed is 3-5 seconds minimum, with progressive pressure that gives the partner clear opportunity to tap.

defender.name: Cross Collar Choke from Body Triangle Defender
defender.description: Learn to defend the cross collar choke from body triangle. Recognition cues, grip fighting strategies, and escape sequences to survive this attack.
defender.overview: Defending the cross collar choke from body triangle is one of the most demanding defensive scenarios in gi grappling. You must simultaneously manage the breathing restriction from the body triangle, protect your collar from deep grip insertion, and work toward escaping back control entirely. The body triangle eliminates the standard hook-clearing escape path, forcing you to solve the collar defense and positional escape as interconnected problems rather than sequential steps. Early recognition of collar grip attempts and disciplined hand positioning are your primary tools for surviving this attack.
key_principles: Protect the collar with at least one hand at all times, preventing deep four-finger grip insertion
Keep your chin tucked and shoulders hunched to reduce collar access around the neck
Strip grips early before both hands are set, as the choke becomes nearly impossible to defend once both collars are secured
Manage breathing despite body triangle restriction to maintain mental clarity for grip defense
Work to turn toward the attacker to reduce choke effectiveness and begin guard recovery
Prioritize tapping early when the choke is locked rather than fighting through arterial compression
recognition_cues: Attacker releases seatbelt or upper body control to begin feeding a hand over your shoulder toward the collar
You feel fingers sliding inside your collar fabric on one side of your neck, pulling the collar tight against your skin
Attacker's elbow drives down toward their hip after gripping your collar, removing slack from the fabric
Body triangle squeeze intensifies as the attacker uses leg pressure to distract you from collar defense
Second hand begins working toward the opposite collar, creating a crossed-grip configuration across your throat

defensive_options.action: Two-on-one grip strip: grab the attacker's wrist with both hands and peel their fingers from your collar before the second grip is established
defensive_options.when_to_use: As soon as you feel the first hand entering your collar, before the grip is set deep
defensive_options.if_successful: Removes the immediate choking threat and forces attacker to restart grip work
defensive_options.risk: Both hands on their wrist means your neck is temporarily exposed to RNC if they switch attacks

defensive_options.action: Chin tuck and shoulder hunch: drop chin deep into chest and raise shoulders to block collar entry around the neck
defensive_options.when_to_use: When you sense the attacker beginning to work collar grips but before fingers enter the collar
defensive_options.if_successful: Creates a physical barrier preventing deep collar grip insertion, buying time for escape work
defensive_options.risk: Purely defensive posture that does not advance your escape and can be overcome with persistent grip work

defensive_options.action: Turn into attacker: rotate your torso toward the attacker to face them, disrupting back control and collar angle
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the attacker commits both hands to collar work, reducing their ability to control your upper body
defensive_options.if_successful: Escapes back control entirely and recovers to a guard position
defensive_options.risk: If the body triangle holds during the turn, you may expose your neck to a different choking angle

defensive_options.action: Frame on the choking arm: insert your forearm across the attacker's forearm to block the finishing motion
defensive_options.when_to_use: When both collar grips are set and the attacker begins pulling elbows back to finish the choke
defensive_options.if_successful: Prevents the choke from tightening to a finishing level, creating time to work grip strips
defensive_options.risk: Late-stage defense with lower success rate than early grip prevention

escape_paths: Strip collar grips early using two-on-one defense, then work to clear body triangle through hip movement and figure-four lock attacks
Turn into the attacker by rotating toward them, using the turn to disrupt collar alignment and recover to closed guard or half guard
Attack the body triangle lock by pushing the foot out from behind the knee, removing positional control before addressing collar grips

favorable_outcomes.how: Successfully turn into the attacker while stripping collar grips, recovering to closed guard where you are now the top player in their guard
Strip both collar grips through disciplined hand fighting, forcing the attacker back to neutral body triangle control without an active choke threat

common_errors.error: Ignoring collar grip attempts while focusing exclusively on clearing the body triangle
common_errors.consequence: Attacker sets both collar grips uncontested and finishes the choke before you address the body triangle lock
common_errors.correction: Prioritize collar defense first, as the choke is the immediate finishing threat. Address body triangle escape after neutralizing the choking hands.

common_errors.error: Using both hands to fight the body triangle while leaving collar completely undefended
common_errors.consequence: Attacker feeds deep collar grips freely while you attack their legs, leading to rapid submission
common_errors.correction: Always keep at least one hand defending the collar. Use one hand for grip defense and the other for body triangle work, or alternate strategically.

common_errors.error: Panicking and pulling on collar grips with maximum strength instead of technical grip strips
common_errors.consequence: Wastes energy under breathing restriction without effectively removing deep collar grips, leading to exhaustion and eventual submission
common_errors.correction: Use two-on-one technique to isolate individual fingers and peel grips methodically. Target the weakest points of the grip rather than fighting the entire hand.

common_errors.error: Failing to tap early when the blood choke is locked and tightening
common_errors.consequence: Blood chokes cause unconsciousness within seconds of full application, making late taps dangerous to your health
common_errors.correction: Recognize when both collar grips are set deep with proper wrist positioning and tap immediately if you cannot prevent the finishing motion.

flashcards.question: How do you recognize that the cross collar choke from body triangle is being set up?
flashcards.answer: The primary cue is the attacker releasing their seatbelt or upper body control to begin feeding a hand over your shoulder toward your collar. You will feel fingers entering your collar fabric and the attacker pulling slack from the material. Increased body triangle squeeze pressure often accompanies collar grip attempts as a distraction tactic.

flashcards.question: What is the safest way to tap to the cross collar choke from body triangle?
flashcards.answer: Tap clearly and early using any available signal: verbal tap, hand tap on the attacker's body or mat, or foot tap. Because the body triangle restricts torso movement, ensure you can reach the attacker or mat with at least one hand. If your hands are trapped, use a verbal tap immediately. Do not wait to see if you can escape a locked blood choke, as unconsciousness can occur within seconds.

flashcards.question: Why should collar grip defense be prioritized over body triangle escape when the attacker begins collar work?
flashcards.answer: The cross collar choke is the immediate finishing threat that can end the match in seconds. The body triangle, while uncomfortable, is a controlling position that does not directly produce a submission. Addressing the body triangle while ignoring collar grips allows the attacker to set up an uncontested choke, whereas defending the collar first neutralizes the immediate danger and gives you time to work the positional escape.

flashcards.question: What defensive options are available once both collar grips are already set deep?
flashcards.answer: Once both grips are set, your options are limited but not zero. Frame your forearm across the attacker's forearm to block the finishing motion. Attempt to peel the most recently set grip using two-on-one technique. Turn aggressively into the attacker to change the choking angle. If the elbows are already retracting and pressure is building on your carotid arteries, tap immediately rather than risking unconsciousness.

flashcards.question: Your attacker switches between collar grip attempts and rear naked choke setups - how should you adjust your defense?
flashcards.answer: Keep one hand always positioned to defend the neck and the other fighting collar grips. When the attacker switches to RNC, redirect your collar-defense hand to neck protection. When they switch back to collar, move one hand to collar defense. Avoid committing both hands to one threat, as this opens the other submission pathway. Accept that you cannot fully prevent both attacks and focus on surviving long enough to create an escape opportunity.

flashcards.question: How does your body angle affect the effectiveness of the cross collar choke being applied to you?
flashcards.answer: Turning your torso toward the attacker's body reduces the scissoring angle of their crossed wrists against your carotid arteries, making the choke significantly less effective. Staying flat or angled away maximizes the attacker's mechanical advantage and choke tightness. Even a partial turn of 30-45 degrees disrupts the collar alignment and buys time for grip fighting. Use this angle change in combination with grip strips rather than relying on turning alone.

flashcards.question: When is attempting to turn into the attacker the right defensive choice versus staying in position and grip fighting?
flashcards.answer: Turn into the attacker when they have committed both hands to collar work, as this means they have minimal upper body control to prevent your rotation. If only one collar grip is set and their other hand maintains seatbelt or upper body control, stay in position and focus on stripping the single grip before it becomes a completed choke. Turning against a strong seatbelt grip often fails and wastes energy, while turning against a two-handed collar attack exploits their over-commitment to the finish.

flashcards.question: How should you manage the compounding effect of breathing restriction from the body triangle while defending collar grips?
flashcards.answer: Take controlled, shallow chest breaths rather than attempting deep diaphragmatic breathing that the body triangle restricts. Avoid holding your breath during grip fights, as this accelerates oxygen depletion and panic. Work in measured bursts of grip defense followed by brief recovery moments rather than sustained maximum effort. Recognize that your timeline is limited by oxygen management and make decisive defensive choices rather than passive resistance that prolongs time under compounding pressure.

training_progressions.focus: Identifying collar grip attempts and strip technique
training_progressions.description: Partner establishes body triangle and works collar grips at 30% speed. Practice recognizing grip insertion early and applying two-on-one strips. Focus on timing and hand positioning rather than strength.

training_progressions.focus: Chin tuck, shoulder positioning, and breathing management
training_progressions.description: Partner applies body triangle with moderate squeeze and works collar grips at 50% intensity. Practice maintaining defensive posture while managing breathing restriction. Develop comfort under compounding pressure.

training_progressions.focus: Combining collar defense with escape attempts
training_progressions.description: Partner attacks at 70% intensity. Practice defending collar grips while simultaneously working to clear body triangle or turn into attacker. Develop the ability to address both the submission threat and positional escape concurrently.

training_progressions.focus: Full resistance defensive rounds from body triangle
training_progressions.description: Partner attacks freely with cross collar choke, RNC, and other submissions from body triangle at full intensity. Practice surviving the attack chain, making intelligent defensive choices, and finding escape opportunities under realistic conditions.
